name: Nilutamide
lead: Nilutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen taken by mouth. It blocks the androgen receptor, the docking site through which testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act on skin, hair follicles and other tissues. Because androgen signalling in scalp follicles and sebaceous glands is central to male-pattern hair loss and oily, acne-prone skin, nilutamide is discussed in appearance communities as a receptor blocker in the same family as flutamide and bicalutamide.[1][2]

It is a prescription medicine approved for metastatic prostate cancer, where it is used together with surgical castration.[3] Its use for hair or skin is not an approved indication. Published work on the drug is almost entirely in prostate cancer, including randomised trials of castration with and without nilutamide and a large meta-analysis of maximum androgen blockade.[4][5]
Its long half-life of roughly two days allows once-daily dosing.[6] Documented risks, including interstitial pneumonitis and visual adaptation changes, are described in its label.[3]

chain: Reduces DHT and testosterone signalling in follicles and skin
Proponents expect less androgen-driven shedding and oiliness
angle.text: Nilutamide blocks the androgen receptor, which is the same pathway that drives male-pattern hair loss and sebum production. Community interest follows from that mechanism; the drug itself is prescribed for prostate cancer.

infobox: About 56 hours on repeated dosing (range reported 23-87 h)[6]
Metastatic prostate cancer with surgical castration (US)[3]

paras: Nilutamide is indicated in the United States for metastatic (stage D2) prostate cancer in combination with surgical castration, with treatment starting on the day of or the day after the procedure.[3] It has also been used alongside GnRH-analogue therapy to blunt the temporary testosterone flare at the start of that treatment, and a trial of buserelin with nilutamide examined this effect.[6][7]

Androgen-receptor blockers are of interest for hair and skin because receptor activation by DHT shrinks susceptible scalp follicles and stimulates sebaceous glands. Reference summaries of nilutamide note that it has been studied for acne and seborrhoea in women and for body-hair reduction and breast development in transgender women, with facial hair little affected.[8] Nilutamide is not approved for any of these uses.

Nilutamide competes with androgens at the androgen receptor and does not itself lower testosterone; blood testosterone can rise through feedback on the pituitary, which is why it is paired with castration or GnRH analogues in cancer care.[1][8] It does not inhibit 5-alpha-reductase.[8]

It is absorbed rapidly after oral dosing. In healthy volunteers the terminal half-life was reported at 43-49 hours, and in prostate-cancer patients about 56 hours; metabolism proceeds largely by reduction of the nitro group.[6]

The US label carries a boxed warning for interstitial pneumonitis, reported in about 2% of patients in controlled trials and in a higher proportion in a small Japanese study; rare cases of pulmonary fibrosis leading to hospitalisation or death have been reported.[3] Other documented effects include delayed dark adaptation, alcohol intolerance, hot flashes, nausea, breast tenderness and liver enzyme changes; liver injury, including rare severe cases, is described in the label and in reviews of nitroaromatic drugs.[3][8][9] The label notes that animal reproduction studies have not been conducted.[3]

Nilutamide was developed by Roussel and first described in 1977, entered medical use in France in 1987 under the name Anandron, and reached the US market in 1996.[8] It has since been largely supplanted in prostate cancer care by bicalutamide and enzalutamide, while remaining on the WHO essential medicines list as an alternative.[8]

Three multicentre placebo-controlled trials of castration plus nilutamide involving 248 patients reported less bone pain, better performance status and more objective regression than castration alone.[10] A multinational double-blind trial of orchiectomy with nilutamide or placebo and the International Anandron Study Group long-term follow-up examined survival and PSA normalisation.[11][12] A review concluded that nilutamide improved response with orchiectomy without improving survival in those trials.[2] The Prostate Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group meta-analysis of 27 randomised trials (8,275 men) compared maximum androgen blockade with androgen suppression alone.[5] No studies found examining nilutamide for hair loss or acne in men.

timeline.event: Trial reports nilutamide preventing the buserelin flare in metastatic prostate cancer.[7]
Becomes available in the United States.[8]

lore.intro: In hair and skin discussions nilutamide appears as one of several antiandrogens, usually next to flutamide and bicalutamide. Few community threads centre on it.

claims.claim: Blocking the androgen receptor could slow androgen-driven hair loss
claims.believers: Proponents of antiandrogens reason that if DHT's action at the follicle is blocked, miniaturisation should slow, as with other receptor blockers.
claims.experts: No published studies have tested nilutamide for hair loss; published research is in prostate cancer.[2]

claims.claim: It could reduce oily skin and acne
claims.believers: Users reason from the receptor mechanism that sebum output should fall.
claims.experts: Reference summaries note studies of nilutamide in acne and seborrhoea in women; it is not approved for these.[8]

claims.claim: It is safer for the liver than flutamide
claims.believers: Some discussion treats nilutamide as a gentler relative of flutamide.
claims.experts: Reference summaries describe liver risk as lower than flutamide but still present, and the label lists a boxed warning for lung inflammation.[3][8]

card.summary: A prescription antiandrogen that blocks androgen receptors, the pathway behind pattern hair loss and oily skin.
card.note: Prescription drug with a boxed warning for lung inflammation; approved only for prostate cancer.

quick.overview:
Nilutamide is an oral antiandrogen approved for metastatic prostate cancer. It blocks the receptor that testosterone and DHT act on.

People interested in hair and skin look at it because that same receptor drives pattern hair loss and sebum production. It is related to flutamide and bicalutamide.
quick.mechanism: It competes with androgens at the androgen receptor without lowering testosterone itself, and has a half-life of about two days.
quick.risks: The label has a boxed warning for interstitial pneumonitis and also lists delayed dark adaptation, alcohol intolerance, hot flashes and liver effects. It is prescription only.
